mainTopic: Using town property under a נדר by writing one's share to the נשיא, and giving a gift through a third person to get around a נדר
overview: The amud opens with the end of a משנה about two people forbidden by a נדר to benefit from each other. Things belonging to עולי בבל, like the הר הבית, are allowed to them. Things belonging to their town, like the בית הכנסת and the bathhouse, are forbidden. The fix is to write one's share of town property over to the נשיא. רבי יהודה and the חכמים argue about whether a formal transfer is needed. A ברייתא explains why the people of the גליל were already covered: they were quarrelsome, so their fathers signed their shares over ahead of time. A new משנה teaches that a person may give food to a third person as a gift, so that someone under a נדר can eat it. The story of a man in בית חורון shows the limit of this method: a gift the receiver could not make הקדש is not a real gift. The גמרא explains that the story illustrates a missing line about gifts that later turn out to be fake. רבא then discusses which wordings make such a gift forbidden, in two versions.

steps.title: Town property is forbidden, with examples
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that people forbidden by a נדר from benefiting from each other may not use the town's shared property. It gives examples of property belonging to עולי בבל and of property belonging to the town.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they are forbidden to use things belonging to that town. What are things belonging to עולי בבל? The הר הבית, the עזרות, and the cistern in the middle of the road. What are things belonging to that town? The town square, the bathhouse, the בית הכנסת, the ark, and the ספרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its rule about shared property. Things of the town are forbidden, and it explains which things count as עולי בבל property and which count as town property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Things of עולי בבל belong to all Jews, so neither person really owns a share, and both may use them. Town property belongs to the residents together. Using it means using the other person's share, which is forbidden benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who came up from Babylonia; their property belongs to all of כלל ישראל
The Temple Mount
The Temple courtyards
The town square
The ark that holds the ספרי תורה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two lists. עולי בבל things (הר הבית, עזרות, the road cistern) are allowed. Only town things are forbidden.

phrases.english: And they are forbidden to use something belonging to that town.
phrases.notes: "They" are two people a נדר forbids from benefiting from each other. Just before this, the משנה let them use עולי בבל property.

phrases.english: And what is something belonging to those who came up from Babylonia?
For example, the Temple Mount and the Temple courtyards,
and the water cistern in the middle of the road.
And what is something belonging to that town?
For example, the town square and the bathhouse,
and the synagogue, the ark, and the Torah scrolls.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's rule from the previous daf about shared property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People forbidden by a נדר from benefiting from each other may use עולי בבל property but not town property.

steps.title: Writing one's share to the נשיא
steps.stepSummary: The משנה mentions someone who writes his share of the town property over to the נשיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who writes his share over to the נשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a short clause about someone who signs his share of the town property over to the נשיא. This sets up both the dispute that follows and the גמרא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the clause looks like one more item on the forbidden list. That reading makes no sense, and the גמרא will ask about it. Giving away your share means you no longer own any part of the town property.

keyTerms.meaning: Writes, meaning signs something over in writing
His share of the town's shared property
The head of the Jewish community

phrases.english: And one who writes his share over to the נשיא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a clause right after the list of town property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing one's share to the נשיא is mentioned in connection with town property.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: writing to the נשיא or to an ordinary person
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the share may be written either to the נשיא or to an ordinary person. To the נשיא no formal transfer is needed, but to an ordinary person it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: it works whether one writes to the נשיא or to an ordinary person. What is the difference between them? One who writes to the נשיא does not need to transfer it formally. To an ordinary person, he must transfer it formally.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה widens the rule. Writing your share to anyone works, but only the נשיא gets it without a formal act of transfer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both options remove the person's ownership of the town property. The difference is procedure. For a הדיוט, a proper transfer (זכייה) is required. For the נשיא, writing alone is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: An ordinary person, not an official
To formally transfer ownership, often through another person who acquires it on the receiver's behalf

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא, וְאֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט.
phrases.english: The same applies to one who writes to the נשיא and one who writes to an ordinary person.

phrases.aramaic: מָה בֵּין כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא לַכּוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט?
phrases.english: What is the difference between one who writes to the נשיא and one who writes to an ordinary person?
That one who writes to the נשיא does not need to formally transfer it,
but to an ordinary person, he must formally transfer it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא, וְאֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the clause about writing to the נשיא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Writing to a נשיא or to a הדיוט both work. Only a הדיוט requires a formal transfer.

steps.title: The חכמים: both require a formal transfer
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say a formal transfer is needed for both. The משנה mentioned the נשיא only because that was the common practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: both this one and that one require a formal transfer. They mentioned the נשיא only because that is what usually happens.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים disagree with רבי יהודה. The נשיא gets no special treatment, and both cases need זכייה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה treated the נשיא as a special case. The חכמים say the משנה named him only because people normally gave their share to the נשיא, not because the law is different for him.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of Sages
They only spoke about, meaning the example was chosen for a reason other than law
About what usually happens; the common case

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה צְרִיכִין לְזַכּוֹת,
phrases.english: Both this one and that one need to formally transfer it,
they spoke of the נשיא only because it was the common practice.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה צְרִיכִין לְזַכּוֹת
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both a נשיא and a הדיוט require a formal transfer. The נשיא is mentioned only as the common case.
steps.whyThisMatters: "לא דברו אלא בהוה" is a common way of reading a ruling: an example can reflect common practice without creating a special legal rule.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: the people of the גליל need not write
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the people of the גליל don't have to write their share to the נשיא, because their fathers already did it for them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: the people of the גליל do not need to write, because their fathers already wrote it for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a special rule for the people of the גליל. Their shares were already signed over by an earlier generation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of writing is to give up ownership of the town property. In the גליל, the fathers already did this on their children's behalf, so the current residents own no share and need to take no new action.

keyTerms.meaning: The people of the Galilee region
Their fathers, the earlier generation
On their behalf, for them

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's solution is to sign your share of town property over, usually to the נשיא. רבי יהודה and the חכמים argue only about whether a formal transfer is needed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
The people of the Galilee do not need to write,
because their fathers already wrote it for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵין אַנְשֵׁי גָלִיל צְרִיכִין לִכְתּוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a special application of the writing rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The people of the גליל are exempt from writing because their fathers already signed their shares over.

steps.title: Why would writing to the נשיא be forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה seems to list writing one's share to the נשיא as something forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the משנה. The clause about writing to the נשיא sits right after the forbidden list, as if it were forbidden too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a person gives away his share, he no longer owns part of the town property. That should make things better, not create a new prohibition. So the simple reading of the clause doesn't make sense.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Why?
Is it forbidden

phrases.english: GEMARA: Why is it forbidden?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is reading "one who writes his share to the נשיא" as part of the forbidden list, and asks why.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Writing away one's share should remove the problem, so it makes no sense to list it as forbidden.

steps.title: רב ששת: the clause is the remedy
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the משנה means: the way to fix the problem is for them to write their shares to the נשיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: this is what the משנה is teaching. What is their remedy? They should write their share over to the נשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question. The clause is not part of the forbidden list. It is the solution that lets them use town property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is read as if it says "ומה תקנתן." Once each person writes his share to the נשיא, neither owns part of the town property. Using it is then no longer benefit from the other person.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is teaching; a reading that explains the משנה's meaning
Their remedy, their fix

steps.whatToRemember: "והכותב חלקו לנשיא" is the remedy, not a prohibition.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: this is what it is teaching:
And what is their remedy?
They should write their share over to the נשיא.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause was a continuation of the forbidden list.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause teaches the remedy: write your share to the נשיא.

steps.title: The גמרא quotes the dispute again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes again the dispute between רבי יהודה and the חכמים about whether a formal transfer is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: it works whether one writes to the נשיא or to an ordinary person. What is the difference? To the נשיא, no formal transfer is needed. To an ordinary person, a formal transfer is needed. And the חכמים say: both require a formal transfer. They mentioned the נשיא only because it was common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה word for word, continuing its walk through the משנה. It does not add any discussion of this dispute here. The next step moves on to רבי יהודה's line about the people of the גליל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is ruled here. The גמרא simply repeats רבי יהודה's distinction between the נשיא and a הדיוט, and the חכמים' reply, as it continues quoting the משנה. Its next comment is about the people of the גליל, not this dispute.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between
Both this one and that one
Need, are required

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא וְאֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט,
phrases.english: The same applies to one who writes to the נשיא and one who writes to an ordinary person,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה בֵּין כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא לְכוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט?
phrases.english: and what is the difference between one who writes to the נשיא and one who writes to an ordinary person?
One who writes to the נשיא does not need to formally transfer it,
and one who writes to an ordinary person must formally transfer it.
And the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה — צְרִיכִים לְזַכּוֹת,
phrases.english: Both this one and that one need to formally transfer it,
they spoke of the נשיא only because it was the common practice.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַנָּשִׂיא וְאֶחָד כּוֹתֵב לַהֶדְיוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the first clause, the גמרא moves on to the next part of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Restates the dispute: רבי יהודה says only a הדיוט needs זכייה, while the חכמים say both need it.

steps.title: Why the fathers of the גליל wrote their shares to the נשיא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's line from the משנה and brings a ברייתא explaining it: the people of the גליל were quarrelsome and often made vows against each other, so their fathers gave their shares to the נשיא ahead of time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says the people of the גליל do not need to transfer their shares, because their fathers already did it for them. A ברייתא explains: the people of the גליל were quarrelsome and kept vowing not to benefit from each other. So their fathers wrote their shares of the public property over to the נשיא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's words from the משנה again so it can explain them with a ברייתא. The ברייתא gives the background story behind his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quote itself was already discussed in Step 5. What is new here is the reason the fathers did this: people in the גליל often made נדרים of הנאה against each other. Once the shares belonged to the נשיא, people could keep using public property without benefiting from the person they had vowed against.

keyTerms.meaning: Quarrelsome people who pick fights
Making a vow that forbids getting any benefit from someone
Their shares (here, their shares of the town's public property)

steps.whatToRemember: The fathers in the גליל gave their shares of public property to the נשיא ahead of time. Because of this, their children's frequent vows against each other would not stop them from using public property.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
The people of the Galil do not need to transfer ownership,
because their fathers already wrote it over for them.
It was taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Yehuda says:
The people of the Galil were quarrelsome,
and they would vow not to benefit from one another,
so their fathers got up
and wrote their shares over to the Nasi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבי יהודה's view from the משנה and explains its background with a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fathers in the גליל transferred their public-property shares to the נשיא because their quarrelsome children often vowed against each other.

steps.title: Feeding someone under a vow by giving a gift to a third person
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if someone is forbidden by a נדר to benefit from his friend and has nothing to eat, the friend may give food to a third person as a gift, and the person under the vow may eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person is forbidden by a vow to benefit from his friend and has nothing to eat, the friend may give the food to someone else as a gift, and then the person under the vow may eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches a way to help a hungry person who is forbidden to benefit from his friend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food goes through a third person. Once the third person truly owns it, the hungry man is benefiting from the third person, not from the friend he vowed against. Because of this, the food is permitted to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
Someone who is forbidden by a vow from getting benefit
As a gift
And that one (the person under the vow)

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who is forbidden by a vow to benefit from his fellow
and he has nothing to eat —
he gives it to someone else as a gift,
phrases.notes: The one doing the giving is the friend who owns the food, not the hungry man.

phrases.english: and that one is permitted to it.
phrases.notes: "That one" is the hungry man under the vow. He may now eat the food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food given as a gift to a third person is permitted to the person who is under the vow.

steps.title: The son in בית חורון gives his wedding meal to a friend
steps.stepSummary: The משנה tells a story. A man in בית חורון, whose father had vowed not to benefit from him, was marrying off his son. He gave the courtyard and the meal to a friend so that his father could come and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man in בית חורון whose father had vowed not to benefit from him. The man was marrying off his son. He said to his friend: the courtyard and the meal are given to you, but only so that my father can come and eat with us at the meal.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה begins a story that tests the rule it just taught. This step sets up the case, and the next step shows what went wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son tried to use the gift method from the משנה's rule. But he attached a clear purpose to the gift: "only so that my father will come." That limit is what causes the trouble later in the story.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a true story brought as an example
בית חורון, a town in ארץ ישראל
Marrying off his son
But only so that

phrases.english: There was an incident with someone in Beit Choron
whose father had vowed not to benefit from him,
and he was marrying off his son.
And he said to his friend:
The courtyard and the meal are given to you,
but only so that my father will come
and eat with us at the meal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story in which someone tries to use the gift method from Step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son gave his courtyard and meal to a friend, but only for the purpose of letting his father eat there.

steps.title: The friend consecrates the gift and explains why
steps.stepSummary: The friend declares the gift הקדש. The son protests. The friend answers that the gift was never really his; it was only a trick to let father and son eat together, and the sin would be on the friend's head.
steps.simpleTranslation: The friend said: If these are mine, they are hereby consecrated to Heaven. The son said: Did I give you my things so that you would consecrate them? The friend answered: You gave me your things only so that you and your father could eat, drink, and make up with each other, and the sin would be on my head.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The friend tests whether the gift is real by consecrating it, and the son's angry reaction shows it was not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the gift had been real, the friend could do anything he wanted with it, including making it הקדש. The son's protest shows he never meant to give it away for real. The friend also did not want to be the one who helped the father break his נדר.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated to Heaven (made into הקדש, belonging to the בית המקדש)
Making up, making peace with each other
The sin hangs on his head (he is to blame)

phrases.english: He said: If they are mine —
phrases.notes: The speaker here is the friend who received the gift.

phrases.english: they are hereby consecrated to Heaven.
He said to him:
Did I give you what is mine
so that you should consecrate them to Heaven?!
He said to him:
You gave me what is yours
only so that you and your father
would eat and drink
and make up with each other,
and the sin would hang on his head.
phrases.notes: "His head" is a polite way of saying "my head." The friend means the blame would fall on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: אִם שֶׁלִּי הֵם הֲרֵי הֵם מוּקְדָּשִׁין לַשָּׁמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story and shows that the gift was not a real one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son's protest shows that the gift was only a trick and not a true transfer of ownership.

steps.title: A gift that cannot be consecrated is not a gift
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים conclude: any gift that the receiver could not make into הקדש is not considered a real gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said: any gift that is not complete enough that the receiver could consecrate it is not a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends the story with the rule the חכמים learned from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test of a real gift is whether the receiver has full control over it, even enough to make it הקדש. The son's gift came with strings attached, so it did not pass. That means the father would still be benefiting from his son.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not a gift
He consecrated it

steps.whatToRemember: A real gift means the receiver fully owns it, so much that he could even make it הקדש. A gift given only to get around a נדר does not work.

phrases.english: The Sages said:
Any gift that is not such
that if he consecrated it, it would be consecrated —
is not a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the rule from the story in Steps 11 and 12.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A gift counts only if the receiver could consecrate it. A gift with strings attached is not a gift.

steps.title: Why does the story contradict the rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the משנה first says the gift method works, but then tells a story where it did not work. Why bring a story that goes against the rule?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is the story brought to contradict the rule?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with how the משנה is built. The story seems to go against the rule at the start of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a משנה tells a story to support its rule. Here the rule allows giving through a third person, but in the story the gift failed. So the story seems to undercut the rule instead of showing it.

keyTerms.meaning: גמרא (marks the start of the גמרא's discussion)
A story brought to contradict?

phrases.english: Gemara:
A story to contradict?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the story in Steps 11 to 13 fits with the rule in Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The structure of the משנה: a rule followed by a story that seems to go against it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A story should illustrate the rule. Here the rule says the gift works, but the story shows a gift that failed.

steps.title: A line is missing: if the end shows the gift was fake, it is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is missing a line. If the giver's later behavior shows the gift was never real, it is forbidden. The בית חורון story is an example of exactly that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Something is missing from the משנה, and this is what it means: if a person's later actions show what he intended at the start, the food is forbidden. The story in בית חורון was a case where his later actions showed his first intention.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by adding a missing line to the משנה. That line makes the story fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gift method works in general. But if the giver later shows it was only a trick, such as protesting when the receiver uses it freely, the gift does not count. The son in בית חורון protested, so his story illustrates this added line and does not contradict the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Something is missing (from the wording of the משנה)
And this is what it teaches
His end shows what his beginning was (his later actions reveal his first intent)

steps.whatToRemember: Giving through a third person works. But if the giver later shows the gift was only a trick to get around the נדר, it is forbidden, as in the story of בית חורון.
steps.confusionAlert: The story does not cancel the משנה's rule. It shows the exception that the missing line adds: when the giver's later behavior proves the gift was fake.

phrases.english: Something is missing
and this is what it teaches:
And if his end shows what his beginning was —
phrases.notes: He means: if what the giver does later reveals that he never meant a real gift.

phrases.english: it is forbidden.
And there was also an incident in Beit Choron with someone,
whose end showed what his beginning was.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 14 by adding a missing line to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: חסורי מיחסרא: a missing line is added to the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story seemed to contradict the rule that a gift through a third person works.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule holds, but there is an exception: if the giver's later behavior proves the gift was fake, it is forbidden. The story illustrates this exception.

steps.title: רבא: Only the 'Only So My Father Comes' Wording Is Forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits the איסור to a case where the son openly said the gift is only so his father can come. If he only said 'let them be yours, so my father can come,' it is allowed, because the choice is left to the friend.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This איסור applies only when he told his friend, 'These are given to you ONLY so that my father can come.' But if he said, 'Let them be yours, so that my father can come,' that is allowed. He is really saying, 'It is up to you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains exactly which words turn the gift into a fake gift that is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'only' (אלא) shows the gift has one goal: to get around the father's נדר. That makes it not a real gift. Without 'only,' the son is simply giving a real gift and hoping the friend invites his father, and the friend is free to decide.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They only taught this when…': a phrase that narrows a ruling to a specific case
'And they are before you': the wording that makes the gift depend on a condition
'By your own choice': it is up to you to decide
My father

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבא is saying the gift idea never works. He is only saying which wording ruins it.

phrases.english: Rava said:
They taught this only
where he said to him: "And they are before you
only so that my father should come."
But if he said to him:
"Let them be before you, so that my father may come,"
it is "by your own choice" that he is saying to him.
phrases.notes: So the friend really owns the gift and can invite the father or not. That is why it is allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the איסור from the בית חורון story to one specific wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the wording 'given to you ONLY so my father can come' makes the gift forbidden. Wording that leaves it to the friend's choice is allowed.

steps.title: Another Version: Even Softer Wording Is Forbidden
steps.stepSummary: In a second version of his words, רבא says the איסור does not depend on the word 'and they are before you.' Even if the son said 'They are yours; let my father come and eat,' it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: Some report that רבא said: Do not think the only reason it is forbidden is that he said 'And they are before you,' and that it would be allowed if he said 'They are yours so my father can come and eat.' No. Even if he said, 'They are yours; let my father come and eat,' it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, stricter report of what רבא said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, only the 'only' wording was forbidden. Here רבא rejects that idea and forbids even the softer wording that mentions the father coming to eat. This version is a real disagreement about how far the איסור reaches. The reason comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Another version': a second report of what a teacher said
'Do not say': rejecting an idea someone might think
Forbidden
Permitted

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new אמורא arguing with רבא. It is a second report of what רבא himself said.

phrases.english: Another version:
some say it this way: Rava said:
Do not say that the reason
is that he said to him "And they are before you"
and that is why it is forbidden,
but if he said to him
"They are before you so that my father may come and eat"
it would be permitted.
Rather, even if he said to him
"They are before you; let my father come and eat"
it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: אָמְרִין לַהּ, אָמַר רָבָא: לָא תֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a stricter version of רבא's ruling than the one in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even without the word 'only,' telling the friend 'let my father come and eat' makes the gift forbidden.

steps.title: The Reason: The Meal Itself Gives Him Away
steps.stepSummary: In this second version, רבא himself gives the reason for his stricter ruling: the wedding meal itself shows that the whole gift was only a trick to bring the father in.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? His meal proves it about him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks and answers his own question, giving the reason for his stricter ruling in this second version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person does not really give away his own son's wedding meal. So the setting makes it clear the gift was never meant to be real, and it was only a way around the נדר. This matches step 15: when the circumstances show the gift is fake, it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is the reason?'
His meal (the son's wedding feast)
Proves about him, shows his real intention

steps.whatToRemember: In רבא's second version, the wording does not save the gift. Since it is his son's wedding meal, the gift is clearly fake, so it is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the circumstances, not only the exact words, can show that a gift was never real.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
His meal proves it about him.
phrases.notes: Nobody truly hands over his son's wedding feast, so it is obvious the gift was just a way to bring the father.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the stricter ruling in step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wedding meal itself shows the gift was only a trick to get around the father's נדר.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why would even the softer wording be forbidden?
